title: Pride, the last thief
hook: ahankar is the last and hardest thief

segments.voice: Yesterday, anger: the burning thief that pushes compassion out of its chair. Your line was breathe first.

A whole morning in the gurdwara shoe room. Rows of sneakers and sandals, wiped and set straight, handed back with a smile. Real seva, done well. Then the drive home, and a small thought slips into the passenger seat: not everyone would have done that. Nothing loud. Just a warm little glow, a quiet tally. The other thieves need some kind of opening. Anger needs an insult. Greed needs something shiny. This one walked in through the good deed itself. Today: pride, ahankar, the thief the title calls the last.
screen: `A MORNING OF SEVA IN THE SHOE ROOM.` → `NOT EVERYONE WOULD HAVE DONE THAT.` → `PRIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ahankar: pride, the swollen I, the self puffed up and asking to be seen. When the Granth names the five thieves, it lists them as lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Pride closes the list. Second, why it's the hardest. Every other thief can be fought, and the fighting itself can feed this one. Beat your anger and you can grow proud of your calm. Give up greed and you can grow proud of your simplicity. Even humility can turn into a trophy. That's one way to read the title: the last thief is the one still standing after you've beaten the others, because it lives on the beating. Third, the Guru's mirror. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says it in one sharp line, in paraphrase: whoever calls himself good, goodness does not come near him. Not, goodness leaves him. It never comes close. Fourth, the hope, in a salok you met early on this path. In Asa di Var, Guru Angad, the Second Guru, speaks of haumai, the ego under pride, in paraphrase: ego is a long, deep disease, but its cure is also within it. The same self that swells can bow. The Gurus' cure is grace and the Name, remembered again and again, and seva that's done and then forgotten. So the seva in the shoe room was good. The tally on the drive home is the thief. The way through isn't to stop serving. It's to catch the tally, smile at it, and hand the credit back to the One who gave the hands.
screen: `AHANKAR: THE SWOLLEN I.` · `IT FEEDS ON BEATING THE OTHERS.` · `CALL YOURSELF GOOD, GOODNESS STAYS AWAY.` · `THE CURE IS ALSO WITHIN.` · then, large: `THE LAST THIEF.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day or two for something you did well, then for the little glow that came after it, the quiet tally: at least I, not everyone would. Don't scold it; catch it gently, the way you'd lift a cat off the kitchen counter, and set it down. On each out-breath, hand the credit back, and if you pray, thank the Lord for the hands that did the work.
Pride. Ahankar, the swollen I, the thief that can feed even on victories over the others; the Gurus say its cure is also within. Today's word.
Your line: the last thief. The same self that swells can bow. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs name ahankar, pride, among the five thieves and counter it with nimrata, humility, through Naam Simran and seva, such as cleaning shoes and serving langar in the gurdwara.
